Unit 8 check

About 20 minutes: one fresh question for each part of every outcome of Unit 8, plus two from earlier units to keep them sharp. It is not graded and only you see it.

An outcome becomes Secure when you have answered a question on each of its parts right first time, without a hint or the solution, here in this check. When all 3 are secure you are ready to try Canvas Quiz 8 (due Sun 6 Dec). Already know this material? Take the check before the lessons and skip what is secure.

8a apply the probability rules to events expressed as sets.

Your answerComplement and addition rules, disjoint events8a

Pick one of the flats to rent in a town at random. AAA: the flat is furnished. BBB: the flat has a garden. P(Ac)=0.72P(A^c) = 0.72P(Ac)=0.72, P(B)=0.44P(B) = 0.44P(B)=0.44 and P(A∩B)=0.07P(A \cap B) = 0.07P(A∩B)=0.07. What is P(A∪B)P(A \cup B)P(A∪B), the probability that the flat is furnished or has a garden (or both)? Give a decimal.

That adds P(A)+P(B)P(A) + P(B)P(A)+P(B) and counts the overlap twice. Subtract P(A∩B)P(A \cap B)P(A∩B) once.
That is P(A∩B)P(A \cap B)P(A∩B), both at once. "Or" is the union, the larger set.
That is the complement, neither AAA nor BBB. "Or" is P(A∪B)P(A \cup B)P(A∪B) itself.
That subtracts the overlap twice, leaving "exactly one". It was counted twice, so remove it once.
That uses P(Ac)P(A^c)P(Ac) as if it were P(A)P(A)P(A). First P(A)=1−P(Ac)P(A) = 1 - P(A^c)P(A)=1−P(Ac).
First the complement rule: P(A)=1−P(Ac)P(A) = 1 - P(A^c)P(A)=1−P(Ac).
Then P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
Solution

P(A)=1−0.72=0.28P(A) = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28P(A)=1−0.72=0.28. P(A∪B)=0.28+0.44−0.07=0.65P(A \cup B) = 0.28 + 0.44 - 0.07 = 0.65P(A∪B)=0.28+0.44−0.07=0.65.

ChooseCheck a distribution by simulation8b

XXX is the number of the 10 patients a drug helps, and X∼Binomial(10,0.4)X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(10, 0.4)X∼Binomial(10,0.4). With rng = np.random.default_rng(), a student runs

x = rng.binomial(10, 0.4, size=100000)

to check P(X≤2)P(X \le 2)P(X≤2). stats.binom.cdf(2, 10, 0.4) gives 0.1673, and the student's simulation gives 0.16817. What do you conclude?

They agree: the gap is simulation noise, and a bigger size would shrink it
Right: with 100,000 draws a share varies by about 0.0012 from run to run, so a gap of 0.0009 is noise.
They disagree by far more than simulation noise: one of the two lines is wrong
A simulation lands close to the exact value, not on it: a gap of 0.0009 is normal for 100,000 draws.
The formula must be wrong: trust the simulation
SciPy's value is exact for the model; the simulation only estimates it.
Set a seed and run the simulation again until the two match
A seed makes a run repeatable; it does not make an estimate exact. Judge the gap against the noise.

8c use a PDF and CDF, find probabilities as areas and find quantiles, with scipy.stats.

ChooseThe PDF: probability is area, not height8c

Adult heights are modelled as N(165,10)N(165, 10)N(165,10), in cm. stats.norm.pdf(160, 165, 10) returns 0.0352. What does 0.0352 tell you?

The height of the PDF at 160 cm: a density per cm, not a probability
Right: probabilities are areas under the PDF. A single value has no width, so P(X=160)=0P(X = 160) = 0P(X=160)=0.
3.52% of the values are exactly 160 cm
That reads the height as a probability. For a continuous model, P(X=160)=0P(X = 160) = 0P(X=160)=0: a single value has no area.
3.52% of the values are at most 160 cm
That would be the CDF, stats.norm.cdf, the area to the left. pdf gives a height.
3.52% of the values are more than 160 cm
That would be 1−F1 - F1−F, an area to the right. pdf gives a height.

8a apply the probability rules to events expressed as sets.

Your answerComplement and addition rules, disjoint events8a

Pick one of 20 flats to rent in a town at random, each equally likely. AAA: the flat is furnished. BBB: the flat has a garden. ∣A∣=7|A| = 7∣A∣=7, ∣B∣=10|B| = 10∣B∣=10 and ∣A∩B∣=2|A \cap B| = 2∣A∩B∣=2. What is P(Ac∩Bc)P(A^c \cap B^c)P(Ac∩Bc), the probability that the flat is not furnished and does not have a garden? Give a decimal.

That is P(A∪B)P(A \cup B)P(A∪B). "Neither" is its complement: 1−P(A∪B)1 - P(A \cup B)1−P(A∪B).
That takes the overlap off twice. By De Morgan, P(Ac∩Bc)=1−P(A∪B)P(A^c \cap B^c) = 1 - P(A \cup B)P(Ac∩Bc)=1−P(A∪B), and the union subtracts P(A∩B)P(A \cap B)P(A∩B) once.
That is P((A∩B)c)P((A \cap B)^c)P((A∩B)c), "not both". Neither is (A∪B)c(A \cup B)^c(A∪B)c: the complement of "or".
For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=∣A∣/∣S∣P(A) = |A|/|S|P(A)=∣A∣/∣S∣.
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
Solution

As probabilities: P(A)=7/20P(A) = 7/20P(A)=7/20, P(B)=10/20P(B) = 10/20P(B)=10/20, P(A∩B)=2/20P(A \cap B) = 2/20P(A∩B)=2/20. P(A∪B)=0.35+0.5−0.1=0.75P(A \cup B) = 0.35 + 0.5 - 0.1 = 0.75P(A∪B)=0.35+0.5−0.1=0.75, so P(Ac∩Bc)=1−0.75=0.25P(A^c \cap B^c) = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25P(Ac∩Bc)=1−0.75=0.25.

ChooseEvents as sets: words, notation, De Morgan8a

Pick a flat at random. AAA: the flat is furnished. BBB: the flat has a garden. Which event is the same as (A∪B)c(A \cup B)^c(A∪B)c?

Ac∩BcA^c \cap B^cAc∩Bc
Right: De Morgan's law: the complement of "or" is "and" of the complements, (A∪B)c=Ac∩Bc(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c(A∪B)c=Ac∩Bc. Both are the event "the flat is not furnished and does not have a garden".
Ac∪BcA^c \cup B^cAc∪Bc
Ac∪BcA^c \cup B^cAc∪Bc is the event that the flat is not furnished or does not have a garden.
A∪BA \cup BA∪B

A∩BA \cap BA∩B

ChooseEvents as pandas masks8a

df holds the 333 penguins of penguins.csv. Pick one at random, each equally likely.

A = df["species"] == "Chinstrap" (it is a Chinstrap)

B = df["year"] == 2009 (it was measured in 2009)

Which expression gives P(Ac)P(A^c)P(Ac), not AAA?

(~A).mean()
Right: the mask is True exactly for the penguins in the event, and .mean() is the share of True.
(~A).sum()
That is a count, ∣Ac∣|A^c|∣Ac∣. .mean() gives the probability.
(~B).mean()
That is P(Bc)P(B^c)P(Bc), not BBB.
(~(A | B)).mean()
That gives P(Ac∩Bc)P(A^c \cap B^c)P(Ac∩Bc), neither AAA nor BBB.

That divides by 16. The SE divides by 16=4\sqrt{16} = 416​=4.

Events as pandas masks

Taught in Lesson 8.1 · Events and probability rules.

Choose8a

df holds the 333 penguins of penguins.csv. Which line gives the probability that a random penguin is a Chinstrap or was measured in 2009?

((df["species"] == "Chinstrap") | (df["year"] == 2009)).mean()
Right: brackets round each comparison, | for "or", and .mean() for the share of True.
(df["species"] == "Chinstrap" | df["year"] == 2009).mean()
Without brackets Python runs | before ==, and the line raises an error. Bracket each comparison.
((df["species"] == "Chinstrap") | (df["year"] == 2009)).sum()
That is a count of penguins. A probability divides by 333: use .mean().
((df["species"] == "Chinstrap") & (df["year"] == 2009)).mean()
& is "and". "Or" is |.

What does the last line print?

0.3

0.7

8

30% of the values lie below 164.8 cm: F(164.8)=0.3F(164.8) = 0.3F(164.8)=0.3
Right: ppf runs the CDF backwards. It takes a share and returns the value with that share below it.

f(164.8)=0.3f(164.8) = 0.3f(164.8)=0.3: the height of the PDF at 164.8 is 0.3
ppf works with the CDF, the area to the left, not with the height of the PDF.

Probabilities and quantiles with scipy.stats

Choose8c

Adult heights are modelled as normal with mean 165 and variance 100, in cm. Which line gives the share of values more than 153?

1 - stats.norm.cdf(153, 165, 10)
Right: SciPy wants the SD, 100=10\sqrt{100} = 10100​=10.
1 - stats.norm.pdf(153, 165, 10)
pdf gives a height, not an area.
1 - stats.norm.cdf(153, 165, 100 ** 2)
That squares the variance. The SD is its square root.
stats.norm.cdf(153, 165, 10)
That is the other side of the value.

1 - stats.uniform.cdf(41, 5, 40)
Right: loc = 5 is the start and scale = 40 is the width, so the answer is 0.1.
1 - stats.uniform.cdf(41, 5, 45)
scale is the width, 40, not the upper end: this is uniform on [5,50][5, 50][5,50].
1 - stats.uniform.cdf(41, 0, 45)
That is uniform on [0,45][0, 45][0,45]: it starts at 0, not 5.
stats.uniform.cdf(41, 5, 40)
That is the other side of the value.

stats.norm.cdf(998, 1000, 4)

The third argument is the SD, 16=4\sqrt{16} = 416​=4, not the variance.

1 - stats.norm.cdf(998, 1000, 4)
That is the other side of the value.

stats.norm.cdf(69, 60, 10) - stats.norm.cdf(50, 60, 10)
Right: the area left of the upper value minus the area left of the lower one.
stats.norm.cdf(69, 60, 10) + stats.norm.cdf(50, 60, 10)
Adding counts the area left of the lower value twice: subtract.
stats.norm.cdf(50, 60, 10) - stats.norm.cdf(69, 60, 10)
The wrong way round: this is negative. Take F(upper)−F(lower)F(\text{upper}) - F(\text{lower})F(upper)−F(lower).
stats.norm.pdf(69, 60, 10) - stats.norm.pdf(50, 60, 10)
pdf gives heights, not areas. Probabilities come from cdf.
